question: Our baby missed the six-week vaccines because of illness. Should we restart all vaccines?
answer:
Please don't restart. Missing the six-week visit doesn't mean starting over. India's immunization guidance says that if a child comes late for the next dose of Pentavalent, Rota or OPV, you give the next dose in the series and don't repeat earlier doses, because there is no maximum interval between doses (INDIA-UIP, p. 15). The first doses of Pentavalent, Rota, fIPV and PCV can still be given up to 1 year of age (INDIA-UIP, p. 7).

A baby with mild fever, diarrhoea or malnutrition can still be vaccinated. Only a critically ill baby who needs hospital care should wait until stable (INDIA-UIP, p. 20).

So take your baby's vaccination card to your doctor or vaccination centre soon, explain the illness, and they will tell you when to give the missed doses. If your baby is still unwell, check with the doctor first.

question: Do I need Td vaccination during pregnancy in India?
answer: Yes, Td (tetanus-diphtheria) vaccination is part of India's schedule for pregnant women (INDIA-UIP, p. 3). Td-1 is given as early as possible in pregnancy, and Td-2 follows 4 weeks later. Td-2 or the booster should preferably be given before 36 weeks (INDIA-UIP, p. 5). At 20 weeks you still have time, so please ask your doctor or ANM soon if you haven't had Td-1. If you already had two doses in a pregnancy within the last 3 years, only one booster dose is needed (INDIA-UIP, p. 5; MOHFW-ANC, p. 26). The shot goes in the upper arm, and mild swelling, pain or redness for a day or two can happen (MOHFW-ANC, p. 26). I can't see your vaccination records, so please check with your doctor which dose applies to you.

question: My glucose test was flagged high. Can I fix gestational diabetes by avoiding rice completely?
answer: I'm sorry the test was flagged. Please see your doctor soon to confirm and plan your care. Cutting out rice completely isn't what the sources advise. The JSSK guidelines say total carbohydrate should be controlled and monitored, not removed. Choose lower glycemic index carbs and avoid refined ones like sweets, juices and sugar. Spread carbs over 3 small meals and 2-3 snacks. Add fibre such as whole grains, pulses, salad and non-starchy vegetables. Avoid fried food, and walk about 30 minutes twice a day (INDIA-JSSK, pp. 29-30). The meal plan depends on your calorie needs, so a specialist should plan it (INDIA-JSSK, p. 30). Treatment usually starts with diet and exercise, and medicines only if needed, and it reduces risks (WHO-ANC, p. 48). I can't say whether diet alone will be enough for you. Please ask your doctor or dietitian, and don't change any medicine without their advice.

question: Can I take an overnight bus at 36 weeks to go to my parents house for delivery?
answer: I don't have a trusted source for whether an overnight bus at 36 weeks is safe. Please ask your doctor before you travel, and ask for your records to carry with you. What my sources do say: complications can develop at any time and aren't always predictable, so delivery at a health facility is recommended (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). Labour before 37 weeks is pre-term labour, and the baby may need specialised newborn care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 81). Because of this, it may help to ask your doctor which hospital near your parents' home you should deliver at, and to plan the trip early. Please contact your doctor or go to the hospital now if you notice leaking or a gush of fluid, fever, foul-smelling discharge, or labour pains.

question: My family says the baby must be a boy based on my bump shape. Is that possible?
answer: I don't have a trusted source that says bump shape can tell whether the baby is a boy or a girl, so I can't confirm it. Please ask your doctor. What my sources do show is that bump size is checked as fundal height, which is how the uterus is measured to see whether the baby is growing as expected (MOHFW-ANC, p. 20-21). That measurement is about growth, not the baby's sex. Please also know that a baby's sex is not something I can predict or help determine. Families sometimes have strong preferences, and WHO notes that preference for a male baby in some places can cause real harm (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 12). Your baby's health matters most. If your family's comments are stressful, it's okay to tell them kindly that you'd rather focus on a healthy pregnancy. At your regular check-ups, your doctor can tell you whether your baby is growing well.

question: I feel anxious about labour and everyone says I should just be happy.
answer: It's completely okay to feel anxious about labour, and you don't have to just be happy. Many first-time mothers feel this way at 31 weeks. The passages don't cover coping with anxiety directly, so for that I don't have a trusted source. Please ask your doctor or midwife. Some things in the guidelines may be reassuring: the birth attendant is meant to give emotional support as well as medical care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39), and you should be able to choose the position that feels comfortable in labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). You can also eat and drink as you wish during labour if you're not likely to need general anaesthesia (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). Labour is watched closely so help can be given on time (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). Try telling your doctor or partner your fears and ask them to walk you through what to expect. If the worry feels overwhelming, or you are not sleeping or eating, please tell your doctor soon.

question: I had a C-section. How should I plan help at home in the first two weeks?
answer:
Congratulations, and well done on getting through surgery. The passages don't give a specific home-help plan for C-section recovery, but they do help with some of the planning. Please check the rest with your surgeon.

Plan for check-ins: WHO recommends at least four postnatal contacts: within 24 hours, between 48 and 72 hours, between 7 and 14 days, and in week six (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152). Home visits in the first week by a skilled health worker are recommended, or clinic visits if home visits aren't possible (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 173). Ask your hospital to book these before you leave.

Plan for food: your helpers can keep meals soft and balanced with plenty of fluids, about 2-3 litres a day including milk, unless your surgeon says otherwise (INDIA-JSSK, p. 10). Calories should not be restricted for long.

Ask for a discharge briefing on wound care, pain and feeding, as women are often unprepared for these (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 91).

I don't have a trusted source for lifting, chores or a day-by-day help roster. Please ask your doctor. If you have heavy bleeding, fever, or worsening pain, contact your doctor or go to the hospital now.

question: My mother-in-law suggests giving honey to my newborn before breastfeeding.
answer: Please don't give honey or any other feed before breastfeeding. Your trusted sources are clear: avoid honey, glucose or water before breastfeeding starts and for the first 6 months (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Prelacteal feeds can delay milk flow and cause illness (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19), and they may not be hygienic and can cause intestinal infections and diarrhoea (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Colostrum, your first milk, is all most babies need at first. It is rich in antibodies and vitamin A and protects against infection (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). Breast milk alone gives all the water and nutrition for 6 months (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). You could tell your mother-in-law kindly that the doctors and nurses advise breast milk only, and that you love her care and would welcome her help with burping, rest and food for you. If the baby seems unwell or isn't feeding, please contact your doctor.

question: I feel I have too little milk on day three. Should I switch to formula?
answer: Worrying about milk on day three is very common, and you're not alone. Please don't switch to formula just yet. Colostrum, the milk of the first 3-4 days, comes in small amounts, and a newborn's stomach is small (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Most mothers can make enough milk, and the more your baby suckles, the more milk you make (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). Feeding on demand, at least 8 times a day, including at night, and checking that the baby is attached well all help (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123; p. 127). Giving formula, bottles or water early can reduce suckling and so your supply (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123). The reliable signs of too little milk are poor weight gain and fewer than 6 wet nappies a day later on (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 121). Please ask your nurse, doctor or a lactation counsellor to watch a feed and check your baby's weight and wet nappies. Contact your doctor or go to the hospital now if your baby is very sleepy, hard to wake for feeds, or has very few wet nappies.

question: My family wants me to eat only rice and rasam after delivery. Is that enough?
answer: Rice and rasam alone isn't enough. After delivery you need more food than usual, especially while breastfeeding, so your body can heal and feed your baby. The MAA guide says to eat about 600 extra calories a day from a variety of foods, 5-6 times a day, with cereals, pulses and vegetables (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). A simple mix like khichri with rice, dal and green leafy vegetables, plus a little ghee, covers a lot. Eat green leafy vegetables daily for iron, add 1-2 seasonal fruits, and include milk, curd, buttermilk, eggs or fish if your family eats them (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177; INDIA-JSSK, p. 20). Drink plenty of water, at least 2 litres a day including soup, milk and buttermilk (INDIA-JSSK, p. 11). You can keep rice and rasam as comforting parts of your meals and add dal, vegetables and curd to them. If you had a C-section or a health condition, follow your surgeon's or doctor's diet advice. Your doctor can help you explain this to your family.

question: Can I give water to my two-month-old in Bengaluru summer?
answer: No, you don't need to give water to your two-month-old, even in Bengaluru's summer. Breastmilk has all the water a baby needs, and exclusively breastfed babies need no water for the first 6 months (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Water is not required even if the climate is hot. Giving water can reduce how much breastmilk the baby takes and raises the risk of diarrhoea (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Water needs of babies even in hot, humid climates are met by the water in breastmilk (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). Feed whenever your baby asks, and dress your baby in 1-2 light layers in summer (MOHFW-ANC, p. 53). If your baby seems unusually drowsy, has very few wet nappies, or is feeding poorly, please contact your doctor right away.
